title: After a Diagnosis: A Practical Guide for Indian Families
description: What to do in the weeks after a dementia diagnosis. Practical, honest guidance on the immediate steps, legal and financial planning, navigating the Indian healthcare system, and how to support the person diagnosed.
author: Project Lantern Editorial Team

sources.name: ARDSI — Alzheimer's and Related Disorders Society of India
Alzheimer's Disease International — Dementia in the Family

body:
const{Fragment:e,jsx:n,jsxs:i}=arguments[0];function _createMdxContent(a){const t={blockquote:"blockquote",em:"em",h2:"h2",h3:"h3",hr:"hr",li:"li",p:"p",strong:"strong",ul:"ul",...a.components};return i(e,{children:[i(t.blockquote,{children:["
",i(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"This article is for educational purposes only."})," It does not constitute medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Please consult qualified medical and legal professionals for guidance specific to your situation."]}),"
"]}),"
",n(t.h2,{children:"The First Days After a Diagnosis"}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"Receiving a dementia diagnosis — for yourself or a family member — is a defining moment. The days immediately following can feel overwhelming: a mix of grief, confusion, fear about the future, and often, a strange sense of relief that the uncertainty has finally resolved into something concrete."}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"This guide is for the weeks and months after the diagnosis. It is practical rather than theoretical, shaped by the realities of navigating healthcare and caregiving in India."}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"There is no single correct path, and every family situation is different. What follows is a framework — not a prescription."}),"
",n(t.h2,{children:"Give Yourself Time to Process"}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"Before making any decisions, allow space for the emotional reality. A dementia diagnosis is a life-changing event. The person diagnosed, and every member of their family, will need time to absorb what this means."}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"Some common emotional responses in the early weeks:"}),"
",i(t.ul,{children:["
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Grief"})," — mourning the future that was imagined, and the relationship as it was"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Denial"})," — difficulty accepting the diagnosis, especially if the symptoms still seem mild"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Relief"})," — if the diagnosis follows years of concerning symptoms, finally having a name for it brings clarity"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Guilt"})," — many family members feel guilty for past impatience or for the relief they feel"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Fear"})," — about what the future holds, about capability to care, about finances, about their own risk"]}),"
"]}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"All of these are normal. None of them require immediate action. If distress is severe, speaking with a mental health professional — or calling a support line — is a reasonable step. See the helplines listed on this site."}),"
",n(t.h2,{children:"Practical Steps: The First Month"}),"
",n(t.h3,{children:"1. Understand the Diagnosis Clearly"}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"Make a follow-up appointment with the diagnosing specialist and come prepared with questions. Consider bringing another family member to help remember and record what is said."}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"Questions to ask:"}),"
",i(t.ul,{children:["
",n(t.li,{children:"What specific type of dementia has been diagnosed?"}),"
",n(t.li,{children:"What stage is it currently at?"}),"
",n(t.li,{children:"What symptoms should we expect in the next six to twelve months?"}),"
",n(t.li,{children:"Are there any medications being recommended, and what are the expected benefits and side effects?"}),"
",n(t.li,{children:"Are there any clinical trials we should know about?"}),"
",n(t.li,{children:"What follow-up appointments are needed?"}),"
",n(t.li,{children:"Where can we find caregiver support in our city?"}),"
"]}),"
",n(t.h3,{children:"2. Share the Information Within the Family"}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"In Indian family contexts, this is rarely straightforward. Decisions about what to tell elderly parents, whether to disclose to extended family, how to handle the social dimension — these are real challenges without universal answers."}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"Some principles that may help:"}),"
",i(t.ul,{children:["
",n(t.li,{children:"The person diagnosed has the right to be part of decisions about disclosure, while they retain that capacity"}),"
",n(t.li,{children:"Hiding a diagnosis from close family members often creates additional stress and limits the support available"}),"
",n(t.li,{children:"Children and teenagers in the household generally do better with age-appropriate honesty than with vague reassurances that something is wrong"}),"
"]}),"
",n(t.h3,{children:"3. Legal and Financial Planning — Act Early"}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"This is the most time-sensitive practical step, and the one that many families delay until it becomes urgent. When the person diagnosed still has full legal capacity to make decisions, certain legal and financial arrangements should be made."}),"
",i(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Power of Attorney:"})," In India, a General or Specific Power of Attorney can authorise a family member or trusted person to manage financial and legal affairs on the person's behalf. While the person has capacity, they can grant this voluntarily. Once capacity is significantly impaired, the process becomes more complex and may require court intervention."]}),"
",i(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Will and succession:"})," If a will has not been made, this is an important time to do so, with the help of a lawyer."]}),"
",i(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Bank and investment access:"})," Understand which accounts, fixed deposits, and investments exist. Ensure a family member has authorised access where needed."]}),"
",i(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Insurance:"})," Review any existing health insurance policies and understand what is and isn't covered for dementia-related care."]}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"Consult a qualified lawyer who has experience with elder law or elder care. This is not a cost that can be safely deferred."}),"
",n(t.h3,{children:"4. Build Your Care Team"}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"No family should try to manage dementia care entirely alone. Building a care team — even a small one — distributes the responsibility and improves the quality of care."}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"Potential members of a care team:"}),"
",i(t.ul,{children:["
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"The diagnosing specialist"})," (neurologist, geriatrician, or geriatric psychiatrist) for medical management"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"A general physician"})," who can coordinate day-to-day health needs"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"A trained caregiver or attendant"})," for practical support with daily activities — particularly as the disease progresses"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"A physiotherapist"})," if mobility is a concern"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"A social worker"})," connected to a hospital or NGO who can help navigate resources"]}),"
"]}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"Hiring a professional caregiver in India varies significantly by city. ARDSI chapters can often provide guidance on finding trained dementia caregivers in your area."}),"
",n(t.h3,{children:"5. Connect with Others Who Understand"}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"The value of peer support — speaking with other families who are on the same journey — cannot be overstated. ARDSI runs support groups for caregivers in many cities. The Dementia India Alliance helpline (8585 990 990) can connect you with support resources."}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"Online communities (including closed Facebook groups for Indian dementia caregivers) can provide a space to ask questions without judgement."}),"
",n(t.h2,{children:"Supporting the Person Diagnosed"}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"A dementia diagnosis belongs first to the person who has it. In the early stages, the person is typically aware, feeling the full weight of what the diagnosis means, and watching for their family's reaction."}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"Some of the most important things a family can do in the early period:"}),"
",i(t.ul,{children:["
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Include the person in planning conversations"})," — for as long as possible, the person with dementia should be part of decisions about their own life"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Listen to what they want"})," — their wishes about care, about where they want to live, about what matters to them, should be recorded and respected"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Maintain normality"})," — continue shared activities, outings, family meals; don't treat the diagnosis as an immediate endpoint"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Avoid talking about the person as if they are not there"})," — even when cognition is impaired, people with dementia retain emotional sensitivity"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Don't correct every mistake"})," — gentle redirection is usually more kind and effective than correction, especially as the disease progresses"]}),"
"]}),"
",n(t.h2,{children:"Looking After Yourself: Caregiver Health"}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"Caregiving for someone with dementia is a years-long journey that takes a significant physical and emotional toll. Caregiver burnout is not a character flaw — it is a predictable consequence of sustained, demanding care without adequate support."}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"From the beginning, build habits and structures that protect your own health:"}),"
",i(t.ul,{children:["
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Sleep"})," — caregiving that disrupts your sleep is not sustainable. Address sleep disturbances in the person diagnosed early."]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Your own medical care"})," — don't defer your own health needs because of caregiving demands"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Social connection"})," — isolation is a significant risk for caregivers. Maintain at least some connections outside the caregiving role"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Ask for help"})," — from family members, from community, from professional support. Many caregivers — particularly daughters and daughters-in-law in Indian contexts — carry a disproportionate share of the burden. This should be named and addressed within families."]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Know the signs of caregiver burnout"})," — persistent exhaustion, resentment, depression, anxiety, and neglect of the person being cared for are warning signs that additional support is urgently needed"]}),"
"]}),"
",n(t.h2,{children:"Resources in India"}),"
",i(t.ul,{children:["
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"ARDSI"})," (Alzheimer's and Related Disorders Society of India): ardsi.org — the national body for dementia in India, with chapters in many cities"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Dementia India Alliance helpline:"})," 8585 990 990"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Tele-MANAS"})," (national mental health support): 14416"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"iCall"})," (psychological support): 9152987821"]}),"
",i(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"NIMHANS"})," (National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences, Bangalore): a leading dementia research and clinical centre"]}),"
"]}),"
",n(t.hr,{}),"
",n(t.p,{children:n(t.em,{children:"This guide was prepared based on publicly available information from established dementia organisations. It reflects the experience of families navigating the Indian context. If you find an error or have a suggestion, please contact us."})})]})}return{default:function(e={}){const{wrapper:i}=e.components||{};return i?n(i,{...e,children:n(_createMdxContent,{...e})}):_createMdxContent(e)}};

title: Understanding the Different Types of Dementia
description: Dementia is not one disease. This guide explains the main types — Alzheimer's, vascular, Lewy body, and frontotemporal dementia — their differences, and why the distinction matters.
author: Project Lantern Editorial Team

sources.name: Alzheimer's Disease International — Types of Dementia

body:
const{Fragment:e,jsx:i,jsxs:n}=arguments[0];function _createMdxContent(a){const r={blockquote:"blockquote",em:"em",h2:"h2",hr:"hr",li:"li",ol:"ol",p:"p",strong:"strong",ul:"ul",...a.components};return n(e,{children:[n(r.blockquote,{children:["
",n(r.p,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"This article is for educational purposes only."})," It does not constitute medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment."]}),"
"]}),"
",i(r.h2,{children:"Dementia is an Umbrella Term"}),"
",i(r.p,{children:"When most people hear the word "dementia", they think of Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's is the most common form — accounting for roughly 60–70% of cases globally — but dementia is an umbrella term that covers a spectrum of conditions, each with somewhat different causes, symptoms, and progression patterns."}),"
",i(r.p,{children:"Understanding the distinctions matters for caregivers and families because:"}),"
",n(r.ul,{children:["
",i(r.li,{children:"Different types of dementia affect different functions of the brain, leading to different care needs"}),"
",i(r.li,{children:"Some symptoms are specific to certain types and may be alarming or confusing without context"}),"
",i(r.li,{children:"The timeline of progression varies significantly across types"}),"
",i(r.li,{children:"Occasionally, an initial diagnosis is revised as the disease progresses and more information becomes available"}),"
"]}),"
",i(r.h2,{children:"Alzheimer's Disease (60–70% of cases)"}),"
",n(r.p,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"What it is:"})," The most common cause of dementia. Caused by amyloid plaques and tau tangles that gradually damage brain cells, beginning in the hippocampus (memory centre)."]}),"
",i(r.p,{children:i(r.strong,{children:"Signature features:"})}),"
",n(r.ul,{children:["
",i(r.li,{children:"Memory loss for recent events is usually the first and most prominent symptom"}),"
",i(r.li,{children:"Gradual, progressive decline over many years (average 8–12 years from diagnosis to end of life, but varies widely)"}),"
",i(r.li,{children:"Difficulty finding words, recognising familiar people, and managing complex tasks"}),"
",i(r.li,{children:"Personality and behavioural changes in middle and late stages"}),"
"]}),"
",n(r.p,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"What distinguishes it:"})," The insidious, gradual onset and the centrality of memory impairment from early in the disease."]}),"
",i(r.h2,{children:"Vascular Dementia (15–20% of cases)"}),"
",n(r.p,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"What it is:"})," Caused by reduced blood flow to the brain — through strokes, mini-strokes (TIAs), or disease of the small blood vessels in the brain. Common in people with high blood pressure, diabetes, or a history of stroke."]}),"
",i(r.p,{children:i(r.strong,{children:"Signature features:"})}),"
",n(r.ul,{children:["
",i(r.li,{children:"Symptoms sometimes appear suddenly after a stroke, rather than gradually"}),"
",i(r.li,{children:'Decline may be "stepwise" — periods of stability followed by sudden worsening after further vascular events'}),"
",i(r.li,{children:"Executive function (planning, reasoning, decision-making) is often more affected early on than memory"}),"
",i(r.li,{children:"Physical symptoms may accompany cognitive changes (weakness, balance problems)"}),"
"]}),"
",n(r.p,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"What distinguishes it:"})," The connection to cardiovascular health, the stepwise rather than gradual progression, and the prominence of executive dysfunction."]}),"
",n(r.p,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"India relevance:"})," Vascular dementia may be proportionally more common in South Asia due to high rates of hypertension, diabetes, and stroke. This is an area where lifestyle risk factor management can make a genuine difference."]}),"
",i(r.h2,{children:"Lewy Body Dementia (approximately 10–15% of cases)"}),"
",n(r.p,{children:["Lewy body dementia (LBD) is an umbrella term that covers two closely related diagnoses: ",i(r.strong,{children:"Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB)"})," and ",i(r.strong,{children:"Parkinson's Disease Dementia (PDD)"}),". Both involve abnormal protein deposits (Lewy bodies) in brain cells."]}),"
",i(r.p,{children:i(r.strong,{children:"Signature features:"})}),"
",n(r.ul,{children:["
",n(r.li,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"Visual hallucinations"})," — often vivid, detailed, and well-formed (seeing animals or people that are not there). These can appear relatively early and be distressing for families who don't understand their cause."]}),"
",n(r.li,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"Fluctuating cognition"})," — alertness and attention vary significantly, sometimes within the same day"]}),"
",n(r.li,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"Parkinsonism"})," — tremor, stiffness, slowness of movement (similar to Parkinson's disease)"]}),"
",n(r.li,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"REM sleep behaviour disorder"})," — physically acting out dreams (sometimes for years before cognitive symptoms appear)"]}),"
",n(r.li,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"Sensitivity to antipsychotic medications"})," — certain medications that are sometimes used to manage behavioural symptoms in other dementias can cause severe, life-threatening reactions in people with Lewy body dementia"]}),"
"]}),"
",n(r.p,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"What distinguishes it:"})," The visual hallucinations and fluctuating cognition are distinctive. The medication sensitivity is a critical safety issue."]}),"
",i(r.h2,{children:"Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD — approximately 5–10% of cases)"}),"
",i(r.p,{children:"FTD covers a group of conditions caused by progressive damage to the frontal and temporal lobes of the brain. It is the most common dementia in people under 65 — sometimes affecting people in their 40s and 50s."}),"
",i(r.p,{children:i(r.strong,{children:"Signature features:"})}),"
",n(r.ul,{children:["
",n(r.li,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"Behavioural variant FTD:"})," Changes in personality and behaviour are prominent early on — disinhibition (saying inappropriate things), apathy, impulsive behaviour, loss of empathy, repetitive behaviours. Memory may be relatively preserved in the early stages."]}),"
",n(r.li,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"Primary Progressive Aphasia:"})," Language difficulties — difficulty finding words, understanding speech, or reading and writing — are the primary early symptom."]}),"
",i(r.li,{children:"Does not typically begin with memory loss"}),"
"]}),"
",n(r.p,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"What distinguishes it:"})," The early prominence of behavioural or language changes rather than memory loss, and the younger age of onset."]}),"
",n(r.p,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"Why it is frequently misdiagnosed:"})," Personality and behavioural changes in an otherwise relatively young person may initially be attributed to psychiatric conditions (depression, bipolar disorder) before dementia is considered."]}),"
",i(r.h2,{children:"Other Less Common Types"}),"
",n(r.p,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"Mixed dementia:"})," Many older people have more than one type of dementia simultaneously — most commonly Alzheimer's combined with vascular dementia. This is more common than previously recognised."]}),"
",n(r.p,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH):"})," Caused by an abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid. Characterised by a triad of symptoms: cognitive decline, gait disturbances (a shuffling walk), and urinary incontinence. Importantly, NPH is potentially reversible with treatment."]}),"
",n(r.p,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD):"})," A rare, rapidly progressive prion disease. Mentioned here only because its speed of decline (weeks to months, rather than years) can be alarming and confusing if the family does not have context."]}),"
",i(r.h2,{children:"Why the Specific Diagnosis Matters"}),"
",i(r.p,{children:"While all dementias share the feature of progressive cognitive decline, the type of dementia affects:"}),"
",n(r.ol,{children:["
",n(r.li,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"Medication decisions"})," — particularly the critical contraindications for Lewy body dementia"]}),"
",n(r.li,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"What symptoms to expect"})," — hallucinations are common in Lewy body dementia but unusual in Alzheimer's; behavioural changes that appear alarming may be a core feature of FTD rather than a crisis"]}),"
",n(r.li,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"Caregiver preparation"})," — different types require different adaptation over time"]}),"
",n(r.li,{children:[i(r.strong,{children:"Research trial eligibility"})," — clinical trials are often specific to certain dementia diagnoses"]}),"
"]}),"
",i(r.p,{children:'If a family member has received a dementia diagnosis, it is worth asking the specialist: "What specific type of dementia is this, and what does that mean for what we can expect?"'}),"
",i(r.hr,{}),"
",i(r.p,{children:i(r.em,{children:"Sources listed below. This article reflects general educational information current as of its last updated date."})})]})}return{default:function(e={}){const{wrapper:n}=e.components||{};return n?i(n,{...e,children:i(_createMdxContent,{...e})}):_createMdxContent(e)}};

title: What is Alzheimer's Disease?
description: A clear, plain-language introduction to Alzheimer's disease — what it is, how it differs from normal ageing, and why an early understanding matters for Indian families.
author: Project Lantern Editorial Team

sources.name: World Health Organization — Dementia Fact Sheet
Alzheimer's Disease International — World Alzheimer Report
ARDSI — Alzheimer's and Related Disorders Society of India

body:
const{Fragment:e,jsx:i,jsxs:n}=arguments[0];function _createMdxContent(t){const a={blockquote:"blockquote",em:"em",h2:"h2",h3:"h3",hr:"hr",li:"li",p:"p",strong:"strong",ul:"ul",...t.components};return n(e,{children:[n(a.blockquote,{children:["
",n(a.p,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"This article is for educational purposes only."})," It does not constitute medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. If you have concerns about memory loss in yourself or a family member, please consult a qualified doctor."]}),"
"]}),"
",i(a.h2,{children:"Understanding Alzheimer's Disease"}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia — a term that describes a group of symptoms affecting memory, thinking, and social abilities severely enough to interfere with daily life. It is not a normal part of ageing, though it becomes more common as people grow older."}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"In India, an estimated 5.3 million people live with dementia, and the number is expected to grow significantly over the next two decades as the population ages. Yet awareness remains low, and many families navigate the journey of caregiving without adequate information or support."}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"This article is a starting point: a grounded, honest introduction to what Alzheimer's disease is, how it progresses, and what it means for the person diagnosed and their family."}),"
",i(a.h2,{children:"Alzheimer's vs. Normal Ageing: What's the Difference?"}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"It is normal to occasionally forget where you put your keys or blank on a name for a moment. This type of forgetfulness tends to improve with prompting — someone mentions the name, and you remember."}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"Alzheimer's disease is different in important ways:"}),"
",n(a.ul,{children:["
",n(a.li,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"Forgetting recent events entirely"})," — not just misplacing keys, but forgetting that a conversation happened an hour ago"]}),"
",n(a.li,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"Getting lost in familiar places"})," — not navigating an unfamiliar city, but losing the way to a shop visited weekly for years"]}),"
",n(a.li,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"Difficulty with familiar tasks"})," — struggling to prepare a familiar recipe, manage money, or follow the thread of a television programme"]}),"
",n(a.li,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"Confusion about time"})," — not knowing the day of the week is common in older adults; not knowing what year it is, or believing long-dead relatives are still alive, is not"]}),"
",n(a.li,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"Language difficulties"})," — finding words less often, in ways that noticeably affect conversation"]}),"
",n(a.li,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"Changes in personality or behaviour"})," — uncharacteristic suspicion, withdrawal, or mood swings that persist"]}),"
"]}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"The key question is always: is this affecting daily functioning in a way it didn't before?"}),"
",i(a.h2,{children:"What Happens in the Brain"}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"Alzheimer's disease involves the gradual breakdown of brain cells (neurons) and the connections between them. Two abnormal protein structures are central to the disease process:"}),"
",n(a.p,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"Amyloid plaques"})," — clumps of a protein fragment called beta-amyloid that build up between nerve cells."]}),"
",n(a.p,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"Tau tangles"})," — twisted strands of another protein, tau, that form inside dying nerve cells."]}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"These changes typically begin in the hippocampus — the region of the brain responsible for forming new memories — which is why memory for recent events is usually the first thing affected. Over time, the damage spreads to other parts of the brain, affecting language, reasoning, and eventually basic bodily functions."}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"Importantly, these brain changes begin many years — sometimes decades — before symptoms are noticeable. This is why ongoing research into early detection is significant."}),"
",i(a.h2,{children:"The Stages of Alzheimer's Disease"}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"Alzheimer's generally progresses through three broad stages, though the pace and pattern vary considerably from person to person."}),"
",i(a.h3,{children:"Early Stage (Mild)"}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"The person can still live independently and participate in most activities. Common signs include:"}),"
",n(a.ul,{children:["
",i(a.li,{children:"Forgetting recent conversations or events"}),"
",i(a.li,{children:"Difficulty finding the right word"}),"
",i(a.li,{children:"Occasionally losing familiar objects"}),"
",i(a.li,{children:"Some difficulty with complex planning or organisation"}),"
",i(a.li,{children:"Mild mood or personality changes"}),"
"]}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"At this stage, many people with Alzheimer's are aware that something has changed. This self-awareness can be painful, and emotional support from family is particularly important."}),"
",i(a.h3,{children:"Middle Stage (Moderate)"}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"This is typically the longest stage and often the most demanding for caregivers. The person requires increasing support with daily activities. Common signs include:"}),"
",n(a.ul,{children:["
",i(a.li,{children:"Significant memory gaps — forgetting names of close family members, major life events"}),"
",i(a.li,{children:"Increasing confusion about time, place, and identity"}),"
",i(a.li,{children:"Difficulty with personal care (dressing, bathing, toileting)"}),"
",i(a.li,{children:"Behavioural changes: wandering, agitation, repetitive questioning, sundowning (increased confusion in the evening)"}),"
",i(a.li,{children:"Sleep disturbances"}),"
"]}),"
",i(a.h3,{children:"Late Stage (Severe)"}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"The person requires full-time care and assistance with all daily activities. Physical abilities decline significantly. The person may lose the ability to speak in sentences, recognise close family, or swallow safely. At this stage, comfort, dignity, and managing pain and distress become the central goals of care."}),"
",i(a.h2,{children:"What Causes Alzheimer's Disease?"}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"The exact cause is not fully understood, but research has identified several contributing factors:"}),"
",n(a.p,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"Age"})," is the greatest risk factor. Alzheimer's disease is rare before 65; risk doubles roughly every five years after that."]}),"
",n(a.p,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"Genetics"})," plays a role. Having a parent or sibling with Alzheimer's increases risk. A specific gene, APOE-e4, is associated with higher risk, though carrying it does not guarantee the disease."]}),"
",n(a.p,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"Lifestyle and health factors"})," — cardiovascular health, physical activity, social engagement, cognitive stimulation, and control of conditions like high blood pressure and diabetes — all influence risk. This is a reason for cautious optimism: some risk factors can be modified."]}),"
",n(a.p,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"Head injury"})," — a history of significant traumatic brain injury appears to increase risk."]}),"
",i(a.h2,{children:"Getting a Diagnosis in India"}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"If you are concerned about memory changes in yourself or a family member, the right first step is a consultation with a doctor. Depending on where you are in India, your options may include:"}),"
",n(a.ul,{children:["
",n(a.li,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"A general physician or family doctor"})," — can do an initial assessment and refer you to a specialist"]}),"
",n(a.li,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"A neurologist"})," — specialises in brain and nervous system disorders"]}),"
",n(a.li,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"A geriatrician"})," — specialises in the health of older adults"]}),"
",n(a.li,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"A geriatric psychiatrist"})," — specialises in mental health conditions in older adults, including dementia"]}),"
"]}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"Major cities have memory clinics and dementia assessment centres, including NIMHANS in Bangalore and AIIMS in Delhi. ARDSI (Alzheimer's and Related Disorders Society of India) maintains a network of support groups and can help connect families with resources in their region."}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"A diagnosis typically involves a medical history, cognitive testing (standardised tests of memory and thinking), blood tests to rule out other causes, and sometimes brain imaging."}),"
",i(a.h2,{children:"What Alzheimer's Is Not"}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"Given how little open conversation there is about dementia in India, it is worth clarifying some common misunderstandings:"}),"
",n(a.ul,{children:["
",n(a.li,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:'It is not "just old age"'})," — while age is a risk factor, Alzheimer's is a disease, not an inevitable consequence of growing older"]}),"
",n(a.li,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"It is not contagious"})," — you cannot catch dementia from another person"]}),"
",n(a.li,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"It is not caused by weakness of character or a spiritual failing"})," — stigma around dementia in India causes real harm to patients and families; the disease is physiological"]}),"
",n(a.li,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"It is not the only dementia"})," — vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia, and frontotemporal dementia are distinct conditions with different presentations"]}),"
",n(a.li,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"A diagnosis is not a reason to immediately withdraw from life"})," — in the early stages, people with Alzheimer's can and do continue to participate in family life, maintain relationships, and find meaning"]}),"
"]}),"
",i(a.h2,{children:"For Caregivers: What This Means for Your Family"}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"An Alzheimer's diagnosis affects the whole family, not just the person diagnosed. Caregiving is a long journey that requires practical preparation, emotional resilience, and help."}),"
",i(a.p,{children:"Some starting points:"}),"

",n(a.li,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"Learn about the disease"})," — understanding what to expect at each stage reduces the shock of change as it happens"]}),"
",n(a.li,{children:[i(a.strong,{children:"Plan ahead"})," — while the person diagnosed can still participate, discuss legal matters (power of attorney), financial plans, and care preferences"]}),"
